item.title: Fiji inflation jumps 7.6% in August
item.description: Fiji’s month-on-month inflation rate compared with the same period last year jumped to 7.6 per cent in August, with consumers facing higher prices for a range of food and non-alcoholic beverages. The Fiji Bureau of Statistics said the 7.6 per cent rate was recorded when the Consumer Price Index for August 2026 was compared with August 2025.
item.content:encoded:
Fiji’s month-on-month inflation rate compared with the same period last year jumped to 7.6 per cent in August, with consumers facing higher prices for a range of food and non-alcoholic beverages.

The Fiji Bureau of Statistics said the 7.6 per cent rate was recorded when the Consumer Price Index for August 2026 was compared with August 2025.

However, the average annual inflation rate for the 12 months to August stood at a much lower 1 per cent.

FBoS said Fiji uses two measures of inflation — one comparing the average CPI over the latest 12 months with the preceding 12-month period, and another comparing prices in the current month with the corresponding month a year earlier.

Despite the sharp annual comparison, the All Items CPI actually fell marginally between July and August.

The index declined by 0.1 per cent from 118.2 in July to 118.1 in August.

Food and non-alcoholic beverages recorded one of the largest monthly increases, rising 2.2 per cent.

FBoS attributed this to higher prices for bread and cereals, milk, cheese and eggs, oils and fats, vegetables and confectionery products.

Consumers also paid more for non-alcoholic beverages, including mineral water, soft drinks and fruit and vegetable juices.

Miscellaneous goods and services increased by 0.9 per cent, while health costs rose 0.3 per cent because of higher pharmaceutical product prices.

Furnishings, household equipment and routine household maintenance also increased by 0.3 per cent, while restaurant and hotel prices edged up 0.1 per cent.

These increases were offset by falling prices in several categories.

Transport recorded the biggest monthly decline at 4 per cent.

Housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels fell by 0.7 per cent, driven by lower liquid fuel prices.

Alcoholic beverages, tobacco and narcotics declined 0.9 per cent, with lower prices recorded for spirits, beer and yaqona.

Clothing and footwear and recreation and culture both declined by 0.1 per cent, while education prices remained unchanged.

The CPI measures average changes in prices paid by households, with monthly price collections undertaken in Suva, Lami, Nasinu, Nausori, Lautoka, Nadi, Ba and Labasa.

item.title: Information vacuum risks confusion over Constitution review: SEEP
item.description: The Social Empowerment Education Programme says withholding the full Constitution Review Commission report is leaving Fijians to “fill in the gaps” and turn to various sources for information about proposed constitutional changes. SEEP executive director Chantelle Khan has called for the immediate release of the CRC Review Report and Draft Constitution Amendment Bill, saying people cannot make inf
item.content:encoded:
The Social Empowerment Education Programme says withholding the full Constitution Review Commission report is leaving Fijians to “fill in the gaps” and turn to various sources for information about proposed constitutional changes.

SEEP executive director Chantelle Khan has called for the immediate release of the CRC Review Report and Draft Constitution Amendment Bill, saying people cannot make informed decisions without access to the complete documents.

“When people do not have access to the full information, they are left to fill in the gaps, turning to various sources that can make it difficult for ordinary citizens to understand what has actually been proposed,” Khan said.

“Make the full report public immediately so that our people can read it for themselves and make informed decisions.”

The CRC handed its Review Report and Draft Constitution Amendment Bill to President Ratu Naiqama Lalabalavu on August 31, but the full report has yet to be made publicly available.

SEEP said the absence of complete information could create confusion and unnecessary concern at a time when Fijians were being asked to consider potentially significant changes to the country’s constitutional framework.

Khan said access to information was fundamental to meaningful public participation.

“People cannot meaningfully participate in decisions that affect their future if they do not have access to the information,” she said.

“Empowering people begins with giving them information.”

SEEP said participation in the next stage should extend beyond political leaders and include young people, women, persons with disabilities, community groups, civil society organisations, traditional leaders, faith-based organisations, workers and businesses.

Khan said every Fijian had a stake in the process because the Constitution determined how the country was governed as well as the rights and responsibilities of citizens.

SEEP also pointed to the use of taxpayers’ money to fund the constitutional review and the public consultations undertaken by the Commission.

Khan said people who participated in those consultations should be able to see what emerged from the process.

“This is not about accepting or rejecting CRC recommendations,” she said.

Rather, Khan said Fijians should be given the complete information before being asked to form opinions on the Commission’s recommendations.

“The public deserves the full information instead of it being meted out in bits and pieces as though serving an agenda we cannot yet see,” she said.

SEEP said greater openness would help reduce misinformation, build public trust and allow for an informed national discussion about Fiji’s constitutional future.

item.title: What needs to be done, FCEF lays out 10 priorities for political parties
item.description: The Fiji Commerce and Employers Federation has outlined 10 major policy priorities it wants political parties to consider when developing their manifestos for the 2027 General Election. In its Private Sector White Paper, FCEF said Fiji’s future economic prosperity would require “bold, evidence-based policy decisions” that encourage private sector investment, productivity, employment and economic g
item.content:encoded:
The Fiji Commerce and Employers Federation has outlined 10 major policy priorities it wants political parties to consider when developing their manifestos for the 2027 General Election.

In its Private Sector White Paper, FCEF said Fiji’s future economic prosperity would require “bold, evidence-based policy decisions” that encourage private sector investment, productivity, employment and economic growth.

The Federation said the private sector would remain the primary driver of economic growth given the Government’s current fiscal constraints.

Among its 10 priorities, FCEF wants political parties to reduce the cost of doing business, improve infrastructure and utilities, reform state-owned enterprises, strengthen trade and exports, protect local industries, overhaul labour market policies, better target MSME assistance, lift productivity, improve education and health outcomes and address Fiji’s declining population.

On the cost of doing business, FCEF is calling for a national review, removal of unnecessary regulatory barriers and the full digitisation of business approval and compliance processes.

It also wants reviews of the Fiji Roads Authority and Fiji Ports, improvements in water infrastructure and measures to reduce electricity costs while accelerating an affordable transition to renewable energy.

FCEF has taken a strong position on trade, calling on Fiji not to sign PACER Plus in its current form and instead seek a review of provisions it believes could negatively affect domestic industries and increase the trade deficit.

To protect local industries, the Federation proposes higher tariffs on imported products that are manufactured locally, while reducing tariffs on raw materials required by local manufacturers for exports and import substitution.

Labour reform is another major priority.

FCEF wants accelerated implementation of Fiji’s National Strategic Human Resource Development Plan and TVET Policy and is proposing that the 40 per cent employers training levy linked to the Work Care Bill be returned to its original training purpose.

It also wants wage and labour law reforms to be based on evidence and take employment and business sustainability into account.

On productivity, FCEF is calling for a national productivity survey and faster adoption of artificial intelligence and other digital technologies across industries.

Education should also be more closely aligned with the present and future skills requirements of businesses, it said, while greater investment was needed in preventative healthcare targeting NCDs, mental health, drug use and HIV/AIDS.

Its final priority calls for Fiji to determine the population size required to maintain sufficient consumption, workforce numbers and economic sustainability and then develop policies to achieve it.

“Fiji’s future economic prosperity will depend on bold, evidence-based policy decisions that promote private sector investment, productivity, employment creation, and economic growth,” FCEF said.

“FCEF therefore encourages all political parties contesting the 2027 General Elections to consider these recommendations as part of a shared commitment to building a more resilient, prosperous, and sustainable Fiji.”

item.title: Tourism earnings fall in June quarter
item.description: Fiji earned $708.1 million from international visitors in the June quarter of 2026, a 4.9 per cent decline compared with the same period last year. Latest figures on Earnings from Tourism show revenue was down from $744.2 million recorded in the June quarter of 2025 — a reduction of about $36.1 million.
item.content:encoded:
Fiji earned $708.1 million from international visitors in the June quarter of 2026, a 4.9 per cent decline compared with the same period last year.

Latest figures on Earnings from Tourism show revenue was down from $744.2 million recorded in the June quarter of 2025 — a reduction of about $36.1 million.

Despite the year-on-year decline, tourism earnings recorded a strong rebound from the first three months of this year.

Earnings in the June quarter were 55.4 per cent, or $252.4 million, higher than the $455.7 million recorded in the March quarter of 2026.

The figures show Australia remained by far Fiji’s largest tourism earnings market.

Australian visitors generated $348.2 million during the June quarter, accounting for 49.2 per cent of total tourism earnings.

New Zealand was the second-largest contributor, generating $155.3 million, or 21.9 per cent of the total.

Visitors from the United States generated $88.5 million, representing 12.5 per cent of Fiji’s tourism earnings for the quarter.

Together with other major source markets, the key tourism markets accounted for 88.5 per cent of total earnings during the June quarter.

The figures highlight the continuing importance of Australia and New Zealand to Fiji’s tourism industry, with the two markets alone generating $503.5 million.

That means more than seven out of every $10 earned from international visitors during the quarter came from the Australian and New Zealand markets.

Fiji’s Earnings from Tourism measure the expenditure of international visitors while in the country.

The figure is calculated using the estimated average daily expenditure of visitors, or per diem spending, together with the total number of visitor days spent in Fiji.

While the June quarter result represents a substantial recovery from the March quarter, the figures show tourism earnings have yet to return to the level recorded during the corresponding quarter of 2025.

Tourism earnings had reached $918.4 million in the September quarter of 2025 before falling to $711.9 million in the December quarter and $455.7 million in the March quarter of 2026.

item.title: Technology, funding unlock remote connectivity push – TAF Chairman
item.description: Changes in technology and economics, backed by Fiji’s Universal Service Fund, have created an opportunity to deliver telecommunications services to communities that have historically been difficult and costly to connect. Telecommunications Authority of Fiji chairman David Eyre said the Universal Service framework had provided the regulatory mandate, while funding and technological developments had
item.content:encoded:
Changes in technology and economics, backed by Fiji’s Universal Service Fund, have created an opportunity to deliver telecommunications services to communities that have historically been difficult and costly to connect.

Telecommunications Authority of Fiji chairman David Eyre said the Universal Service framework had provided the regulatory mandate, while funding and technological developments had now made practical delivery possible.

“The Universal Service provisions gave us the mandate. The Universal Service Fund provided the mechanism. Changes in technology and economics created the opportunity,” Eyre said at the National Universal Service Launch.

“Industry provided the delivery capability. And communities provided the cooperation necessary to make it work.”

Eyre said the development represented an important turning point for efforts to close connectivity gaps across Fiji, particularly in rural, maritime, highland and interior communities.

He said Fiji’s geography had historically made conventional telecommunications infrastructure commercially difficult to deploy in some locations.

Distance, difficult terrain, maritime isolation, small populations and the costs associated with constructing, powering and maintaining infrastructure meant normal market conditions did not always support investment.

“The purpose of Universal Service is to address that gap in a structured and accountable way, based on a simple principle: where a person lives should not unnecessarily determine whether they have reasonable access to telecommunications services,” Eyre said.

TAF had previously explored conventional telecommunications towers for underserved communities, but Eyre said the economics of building and maintaining the infrastructure across numerous small and remote locations could not be made viable.

Satellite technology was another option, but historically high equipment and recurring service costs had made widespread deployment difficult to sustain.

Eyre said those economics had now changed.

More accessible satellite connectivity provided a practical backhaul solution for locations where conventional infrastructure remained difficult to justify, while improved commercial arrangements had significantly reduced the recurring cost barriers previously associated with the model.

“What we are recognising today is therefore not the sudden discovery of Universal Service,” he said.

“It is the point at which policy, technology, funding and economics have aligned sufficiently to turn a long-standing statutory objective into practical delivery.”

Eyre said combining these developments with Universal Service funding and competitive delivery through telecommunications providers meant Fiji finally had a model capable of being implemented at scale.

He said the initiative also demonstrated the need for regulators to evolve alongside technological and market changes.

“Regulation cannot remain static while technology and markets change,” Eyre said.

He said a modern regulator must understand law, technology, markets and economics and identify where normal commercial investment would not deliver the public outcomes required.

item.title: Kumar demands release of Constitution review report
item.description: Opposition MP Premila Kumar has questioned why Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka is asking Fijians to remain calm over the constitutional review process when the public has yet to see the Constitution Review Commission’s report and proposed Draft Constitution. Kumar said the Constitution belonged to the people and argued that the Commission’s documents should be released immediately and in their orig
item.content:encoded:
Opposition MP Premila Kumar has questioned why Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka is asking Fijians to remain calm over the constitutional review process when the public has yet to see the Constitution Review Commission’s report and proposed Draft Constitution.

Kumar said the Constitution belonged to the people and argued that the Commission’s documents should be released immediately and in their original form.

“The Government cannot ask Fijians to trust a constitutional process while keeping the actual documents away from them,” Kumar said.

She also raised concerns over reports that independent media organisations were not invited to witness the formal handover of the Commission’s report at State House, with coverage instead undertaken by the Ministry of Information.

Kumar said this was particularly concerning given the Coalition Government’s commitments to media freedom, transparency and open government.

“This was not an ordinary Government report. This concerns the Constitution — the supreme law of our country and the rights and freedoms of every Fijian,” she said.

Kumar also questioned Rabuka’s call for calm and his assurances to minority communities, including Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs, that their religious freedoms and place in Fiji would continue to be respected.

“So why is the Prime Minister already asking people to remain calm? A call for calm implies that something in the report is expected to cause alarm,” she said.

“The Government should not tell people how to feel about a document they have not seen, nor can they be expected to blindly accept assurances about a document they have not read.”

Kumar said the unresolved question of Fiji’s common national identity also required careful consideration as part of any constitutional reform.

She said any constitutional settlement should respect indigenous identity and traditions while protecting the rights, religious freedoms and equal belonging of all citizens.

Kumar welcomed the President’s assurance that receiving the Commission’s report did not mean its recommendations had been accepted and that the proposals would still have to undergo the appropriate constitutional, parliamentary and democratic processes.

However, she said those processes could not be meaningful without public access to the documents.

“The Government should therefore publish the Constitution Review Commission’s full Report and Draft Constitution immediately in its original form as submitted by the Commission, before any changes are made by Government,” Kumar said.

She said taxpayers had funded the constitutional review and should be able to see what the independent Commission had proposed and distinguish it from any subsequent changes made by Government.

“This process must be bigger than politics. It must be transparent, lawful, genuinely democratic and worthy of the trust of all Fijians,” Kumar said.

item.title: FCEF warns Fiji growth falling short of 2050 ambitions
item.description: Fiji’s economy is not growing fast enough to achieve its long-term development ambitions, while businesses continue to face rising costs, severe skills shortages and increasing vulnerability to external shocks, the Fiji Commerce and Employers Federation says. In its Private Sector White Paper, FCEF said economic growth had been revised down to 1.5 per cent for 2026, before increasing to a projecte
item.content:encoded:
Fiji’s economy is not growing fast enough to achieve its long-term development ambitions, while businesses continue to face rising costs, severe skills shortages and increasing vulnerability to external shocks, the Fiji Commerce and Employers Federation says.

In its Private Sector White Paper, FCEF said economic growth had been revised down to 1.5 per cent for 2026, before increasing to a projected 2.5 per cent in 2027 and 3 per cent in 2028.

The Federation said these rates remained significantly below the estimated 5 per cent annual growth required for Fiji to transition to a higher-income economy by 2050.

FCEF identified inflation, the widening trade deficit, slow economic diversification and legislation that it says impedes business sustainability, innovation and modernisation among major challenges confronting the private sector.

It said Fiji also remained vulnerable to geopolitical conflicts, fuel price volatility and climate-related events, while delays in transitioning to renewable energy continued to leave the economy dependent on imported fuel.

The White Paper also highlighted what FCEF described as a labour and skills crisis, noting more than 114,000 Fijians migrated overseas between 2018 and 2025, including a significant number of skilled workers.

Employers, it said, continued to report critical skills shortages across several sectors, while foreign worker recruitment had increased by 79 per cent over the past three years.

Youth unemployment was estimated at about 18 per cent, while approximately 26 per cent of young people were not engaged in education, employment or training.

FCEF said addressing these challenges would require coordinated reforms across education, training, labour market policy, healthcare and economic development.

The Federation said its White Paper was intended to help shape the manifestos of political parties contesting the 2027 General Election and was not aligned with any particular party.

“Investor confidence and economic prosperity are heavily reliant on political will,” the White Paper stated.

It said political parties needed to recognise that election promises ultimately depended on the country’s ability to generate sustainable economic growth.

“While political parties need to respond to the needs and aspirations of their potential voters, it is important to understand that those campaign promises can only be funded if there are economic growth and stability,” FCEF said.

“Economic growth is only realised if the right business policies are adopted and implemented when in Government.”

item.title: Shed destroyed in fire at Delai Saweni car wash
item.description: A SHED at a car wash and tyre centre in Delai Saweni, Lautoka, was completely destroyed by fire on Monday evening. The National Fire Authority (NFA) received a report of the fire from the National Command Centre at about 5.30pm.
item.content:encoded:
A SHED at a car wash and tyre centre in Delai Saweni, Lautoka, was completely destroyed by fire on Monday evening.

The National Fire Authority (NFA) received a report of the fire from the National Command Centre at about 5.30pm.

According to NFA the property owner was reportedly in Sabeto, Nadi, attending a funeral.

“Attempts to contact the business owner were unsuccessful,” the statement from NFA said.

NFA chief executive officer Puamau Sowane said the incident highlighted the importance of fire prevention and early detection.

He urged business and property owners to properly manage electrical systems, appliances, flammable materials and other potential fire hazards.

Mr Sowane also encouraged property owners to install smoke alarms to provide early warning and allow people to evacuate and alert emergency services.

Investigations into the cause of the fire continue.
